note:
One sent out as an official representative of Christ, exercising authority that He has delegated and receiving new revelation from the risen Lord (Eph. 3:5). See note on 2 Cor. 1:1. This phrase is commonly used by Paul as a self-designation in the openings of his letters.

**God our Savior.** As author of the covenant of grace, God is Savior (2:3; 4:10; Titus 1:3; 2:10; 3:4).

**Christ Jesus our hope.** Jesus is the basis for Christian hope because He is the mediator of the covenant of grace (2:5; 4:10; 5:5; 6:17). See theological note “Hope” on p. 2206.

Cf. Titus 1:4. Paul views Timothy as his spiritual son, who can be trusted to reflect the apostle’s character and perspective, as a son reflects his father’s, in his dealings with churches (v. 18; 1 Cor. 4:17; Phil. 2:22; 2 Tim. 1:2; 2:1; Introduction: Date and Occasion).

**Grace, mercy, and peace.** Paul commonly substitutes “grace” for the more standard salutation “greetings” (literally, “rejoice”; e.g., James 1:1). He typically adds the Jewish greeting “peace,” referring to the peace with God that Christ has secured for His people. Here and in 2 Tim. 1:2, he also adds “mercy.”

Paul moves into the body of the letter, bypassing the expression of thanksgiving or praise to God that is customary in his epistles to churches (except Galatians) and proceeding immediately to Timothy’s pastoral assignment in Ephesus (cf. Titus 1:5). His intention is to instruct Timothy in how to act as Paul’s representative in establishing good order in the church at Ephesus (3:14, 15) and in responding to specific spiritual threats to the believers there (see Introduction: Date and Occasion). Assuming that the entire church will hear the epistle (6:21; see Introduction: Literary Features), Paul intends his directives to substantiate Timothy’s authority to implement Paul’s instructions in the eyes of the congregation. He begins with the problem of false teaching at Ephesus (see Introduction to 2 Timothy: Special Issues).

**1:3 teach any different doctrine.** The conflict in Ephesus centers on proper teaching (v. 10; 4:1, 2; 6:3; 2 Tim. 2:2, 18).

See 4:7; 2 Tim. 4:4. In Titus 1:14, Paul speaks of “Jewish myths,” perhaps referring to the kinds of legends about OT figures that are found in many of the apocryphal Jewish writings.

**endless genealogies.** Perhaps a reference to an early form of the detailed speculations (often combined with Jewish myths) that developed in Gnosticism concerning the origins of the world and the innumerable spiritual beings supposedly involved in creation (cf. Titus 3:9).

**stewardship from God.** Ministers of the gospel, like the slave who is steward of his master’s estate, are accountable to the Lord for their conduct in leadership and preservation of the message of Christ (v. 11; 6:20; 2 Tim. 1:13, 14; 2:1, 2). Above all, the steward must be faithful (1 Cor. 4:1, 2).
Paul’s command highlights the close and necessary connection between true Christian belief and practice (cf. Gal. 5:6).
The law of Moses.

Paul’s comments about the false teachers lead him into a digression on the purpose of the law.

**1:8 the law is good.** See Rom. 7:7–12; Gal. 3:19–25.

verse_quote: the law is not laid down for the just.
note: The law’s commandments prohibit and indict the sorts of sins that Paul goes on to list—violent defiance of parents, murder, sexual immorality, etc. (evils that also contradict the sound doctrine of the gospel; vv. 10, 11). If people’s hearts were intrinsically upright, the law’s stipulations would not be necessary. As it is, however, the law exposes the heart’s sinful proclivity (Rom. 3:20; 7:7, 8). The law also acts an external restraint on sin, holding people back from doing the worst that they can externally even while those whom the law restrains seize on the commandments and break the commandments with abandon internally in their hearts, souls, and minds.

Or “sound teaching,” a theme running throughout the Pastoral Epistles (3:9; 4:6; 6:3; 2 Tim. 1:13, 14; 2:2; 4:3; Titus 1:9, 13; 2:1, 2). The word “sound” implies that true doctrine preserves and promotes spiritual health, unlike false doctrine, which destroys spiritual vitality and spreads infection “like gangrene” (2 Tim. 2:17).
The good news of what God has done in Christ is the standard by which doctrine, as well as one’s understanding and use of the law, is judged to be sound.

From his comments about the law and the misuse of the law by false teachers, Paul turns to his call by Christ and provides an exposition of the gospel as the grace that God pours out upon sinners in Jesus Christ.

verse_quote: a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent.
note:
Before his conversion, Paul persecuted the church (Acts 8:3; 9:1–5; 22:4, 5; 26:9, 11; Gal. 1:13). At that time, he saw it as his obligation in his zeal for God’s glory (Phil. 3:6); but now, having received grace through Jesus the Christ, he views his history as a persecutor as constituting him “the least of the apostles” (1 Cor. 15:8–10); “the least of all the saints” (Eph. 3:8), and the “foremost” of sinners (vv. 15, 16).

**because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief.** God did not grant Paul what he deserved, but what he needed (cf. Acts 3:17–20). Paul did nothing to merit or qualify for God’s mercy in Christ. The apostle is not saying that ignorance can excuse sin, for even those who sin when they do not know the will of the Master receive punishment if they do not repent (Luke 12:35–48).

verse_quote: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance.
note:
This expression calls attention to an important point. In the NT it is found only in the Pastoral Epistles (3:1; 4:9; 2 Tim. 2:11; Titus 3:8).

**to save sinners.** This concise and comprehensive statement of Christ’s mission in His incarnation, focused on the redemptive purposes of His death and resurrection, merits comparison with similar NT statements, including John 3:16; Gal. 4:4, 5; and Heb. 10:5–10.

**I am the foremost.** Lit. “I am the first.” This is not a characterization only of his record as a blasphemous and violent persecutor prior to his conversion. Rather, as Paul has grown in Christ, even as the Holy Spirit has been conforming him to his Savior’s purity and love, he has also become increasingly aware of his own sinfulness.
God grants to all who believe in Christ not just “eternal” life, but life in all its fullness (cf. 4:8; 6:12, 19; 2 Tim. 1:1, 10; Titus 1:2; 3:7).
Jonathan Edwards recalls this text in the account of his conversion. As he read these words, “he had a sense of the glory of the divine being,” and “prayed to God that I might enjoy him.”

Paul returns to the theme of vv. 3–7, focusing less on Timothy’s potential for success as Paul’s representative than on Timothy’s continued faithfulness to Christ, especially in contrast to two members (perhaps leaders) of the church at Ephesus who “made shipwreck of their faith” (v. 19).

**1:18 prophecies previously made about you.** This refers to an event, mentioned also in 4:14 and in 2 Tim. 1:6 (cf. 2 Tim. 2:2), in which a group of elders, along with Paul, laid hands on Timothy (when Timothy was set apart for ministry). At that time, Timothy received a spiritual gift, along with a word of prophecy appointing him for service (cf. Acts 13:1–3).

**wage the good warfare.** In this conflict, victory is perseverance in faith and integrity (v. 19; 2 Tim. 4:7).

Singling out these two individuals raises the question as to whether they were leaders in the church. Hymenaeus is mentioned again in 2 Tim. 2:17, 18 as one who has “swerved from the truth.” It is unclear whether the name “Alexander” here and in Acts 19:33, 34 and 2 Tim. 4:14, 15 all refer to the same person.

**I have handed over to Satan.** This is probably a reference to putting these two individuals outside the fellowship of the church and, hence, back into the world—the domain of Satan (John 12:31; 14:30; 16:11; 2 Cor. 4:4; Eph. 2:2). Paul uses a similar expression in 1 Cor. 5:5 (cf. Matt. 18:17).

**may learn not to blaspheme.** The purpose of this excommunication, like that in 1 Cor. 5:5, is not punitive but, by the Spirit’s convicting grace, restorative—that the two would recognize their errors and repent (2 Tim. 2:25, 26; Titus 3:10).

Paul moves to a series of instructions on prayer and worship, perhaps in response to abuses caused by the false teachers (see Introduction to 2 Timothy: Special Issues). After the instructions for worship, he moves on to the qualifications of church officers (3:1–13), summing up the entire section as directives “how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God” (3:15).

**2:1 all people.** As can be seen from the next expression (“for kings and all who are in high positions”), this does not mean “every human being”; rather, it refers to “all types of people,” whatever their station in life.

verse_quote: all who are in high positions.
note:
Civil government, though led by flawed human beings and vulnerable to corruption and exploitation, is ordained by God to maintain justice (Rom. 13:1–7; 1 Pet. 2:13–17).

**a peaceful and quiet life.** Christ’s name is honored when Christians live peaceably and responsibly among their neighbors (3:7; 1 Thess. 4:11, 12; 2 Thess. 3:12).

verse_quote: who desires all people to be saved.
note: This does not mean that God sovereignly wills every human being to be saved (i.e., that God saves or wishes to save everyone, since Rom. 9:18–24 says otherwise, and speaks of God’s “desire” in expressing His election and reprobation). It may refer to God’s general benevolence in taking no delight in the death of the wicked (Ezek. 33:11) or to God’s desire that all types of people (v. 1 note) be saved (i.e., God does not choose His elect from any single nationality, class, or other group).

This is the fundamental affirmation of both OT and NT religion (Deut. 6:4; cf. Rom. 3:30; 1 Cor. 8:6; Gal. 3:20; Eph. 4:6).

**one mediator between God and men.** There is only one who arbitrates between God and humanity and reconciles them. See theological note “Jesus Christ as Mediator.”

**the man Christ Jesus.** In speaking of Christ as mediator, Paul’s focus is on Christ’s humanity. This may be because the false teachers in Ephesus denied that Christ was truly human. The full humanity of Christ is essential to His serving as mediator of the covenant of grace (Heb. 2:17; 4:14–5:10; 9:13–15).

verse_quote: who gave himself as a ransom.
note:
By His death on the cross, Christ paid the price necessary to free His people from their sins (Matt. 20:28; Mark 10:45; Titus 2:14; 1 Pet. 1:18, 19). This is a centerpiece of His work as the “one mediator” (v. 5).

**all.** In keeping with vv. 1 and 4, this is probably a reference to all _types_ of people (i.e., from every tongue, tribe, and nation; cf. Rev. 7:9). Alternatively, it expresses Paul’s conviction that although Christ’s death was sufficient to ransom all humanity if that had been God’s intent in offering up His Son for sinners, God has never intended to save all people and the purpose of the atonement was to pay only for the sins of the elect. See theological note “Definite Atonement” on p. 1875.

verse_quote: I am telling the truth ... not lying.
note: An odd statement to make to a close friend, but Paul intended for the letter to be read to the whole church (6:21 note). Presumably, the false teachers had questioned Paul’s call and mission.

Paul moves to specific admonitions for men and women in the context of worship (vv. 1–15 note).

**2:8 every place.** The principles governing corporate worship are not limited to a single congregation but are applicable to churches everywhere, although local issues sometimes influence how the principles should be applied. See 1 Cor. 14:33–36.

**men.** Paul assumes in 1 Cor. 11:5 that women, too, will pray when the church meets for worship. Here he may be addressing specific problems at Ephesus, such as conflict among men, and indiscreet clothing and preoccupation with appearance among women.

**lifting holy hands.** On this posture in prayer, see Ps. 63:4; 141:2.

**without anger or quarreling.** Paul is not concerned to mandate a particular posture, but to encourage a proper attitude (1:5).
Paul is not concerned with clothing and jewelry as such, but with the attitude of the one wearing them (1 Pet. 3:3, 4). Greco-Roman society was characterized by extravagance in dress.

As 1 Cor. 11:5 indicates, Paul does not forbid all vocal participation by women in the worship service. Rather, Paul enjoins silence of a particular sort—a silence that respects the authoritative teaching and governing role assigned to the male leaders of the church (v. 12).

**all submissiveness.** Submission does not mean that one is inferior in being to another. Elsewhere, Paul applies the concept to wives (Eph. 5:22; Col. 3:18; Titus 2:5; cf. 1 Cor. 14:34), husbands and wives (Eph. 5:21), children (3:4), slaves (Titus 2:9), prophets (1 Cor. 14:32), Christians (Rom. 13:1, 5; 1 Cor. 16:16; Titus 3:1), the church (Eph. 5:24), and even Christ Himself (1 Cor. 15:28).

Here Paul exercises his apostolic authority in restricting women from exercising a specific kind of authority and teaching, namely that which is associated with the ecclesiastical office of overseer, or elder (3:1–7). This verse indicates that women should not be ordained to the office of elder.

**to exercise authority over.** This Gk. word appears only here in the NT and is used by Paul to refer to some level of judicial or governing authority. Under the influence of the false teachers, certain women have apparently moved into positions of governing authority within the church, which Paul prohibited (1 Cor. 14:34).

**quiet.** See note on v. 11.

Paul appeals to the creation order instituted by God Himself (Gen. 2:7, 21, 22; he uses a similar argument, though with some qualification, in 1 Cor. 11:8–12). As “firstborn,” Adam had the rights of primogeniture, which, according to passages about firstborn sons in the OT, entailed not only inheritance rights but authority over the household. The fact that the apostle appeals to the created order is strong evidence against seeing this teaching about the role of women in the church as limited only to the particular circumstances in Ephesus. From the beginning, as Paul teaches in Eph. 5:22–30. God designed husbands to lovingly lead their wives and for wives to submit themselves to their husbands’ authority, for by this believers illustrate the relationship of Christ, our husband, and the church, His bride (Eph. 5:22–30 and notes). In the church, this relationship is illustrated by the intelligent submission of both women and non-ordained men to those men who have been appointed to the office of elder. Elders are to exercise their authority in a loving manner and not abuse the believers under their care, just as husbands are to love their wives enough to die for them (1 Pet. 5:1–4 and notes).

Again Paul alludes to Genesis, this time to the account of the fall (Gen. 3:1–6). The argument might seem unfair, since both Adam and Eve sinned. But Paul’s point is correct: Eve was the one who was “deceived” by the serpent. Paul’s argument here, with its emphasis on who was deceived, may reflect the relative success that the false teachers at Ephesus were having in leading women astray (5:11–15; 2 Tim. 3:6, 7). Elsewhere, Paul has no qualms about assigning responsibility for the fall to Adam (Rom. 5:12–19; 1 Cor. 15:21, 22).

This probably refers to any woman, not simply to Eve.

**will be saved.** Unlikely to mean “brought safely” (physically preserved through the process of childbirth), as some hold. Paul uses his normal word meaning “redemption from sin,” thereby contrasting being deceived into sin (v. 14) with being saved from it. Alternately, the term “saved” may indicate the reception of some important, though unspecified, benefit from God.

**through childbearing.** The interpretation “through the birth of the Child” (Jesus), however attractive it might be theologically, is doubtful. Paul intends another allusion to Genesis, this time to God’s statement to Eve after the fall concerning her role in childbearing (Gen. 3:16).

**if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.** This qualification shows that Paul is not suggesting that childbearing is an act that merits salvation, which would contradict his doctrine of justification by faith. Rather, his point is that those women at Ephesus who have been deceived by the false teachers, and Christian women generally, need to focus on their proper God-assigned role, and especially on embracing their calling with Christlike attitudes befitting women of faith (vv. 8–10; 1:5, 19). Given his use of Genesis 2; 3 in his argument and the false teachers’ disparagement of marriage (4:3), Paul finds “childbearing” (1 Tim. 5:14) and “bringing up children” (1 Tim. 5:10) to be important symbols for that role (5:14). Ultimately, Paul wants women to understand that they do not have to reject their homes and families in order to have worth in God’s sight or to enjoy all the benefits of redemption; rather, they work out their salvation in fear and trembling (Phil. 2:13, 14) as they fulfill their calling in the home.

Paul now turns to the subject of leadership in the church, continuing his instructions for behavior befitting the church as God’s household (v. 15). He first discusses overseers (vv. 1–7; v. 1 text note) and then discusses deacons (vv. 8–10, 12, 13, with a digression on women in v. 11). Paul focuses more on the personal qualities of those who are qualified to serve in these positions than on their duties. This emphasis indicates his concern to install the right people, perhaps because some of the false teachers in Ephesus had come from, or were selfishly seeking, positions of leadership.

**3:1 The saying is trustworthy.** See note on 1:15. The use of this expression here reflects the importance Paul attaches to the task of the overseer, or elder.

**overseer.** One of a group of individuals charged with the general care of the church (v. 5; cf. Phil. 1:1). The word is used interchangeably with “elder” and describes the elder’s role in providing spiritual oversight in the church (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7). The Gk. term (_episkopos_) is the origin of the En­glish words “bishop” and “episcopal,” but NT usage (unlike later church practice) shows that each congregation had a plurality of elders who held each other accountable with shared authority (Acts 20:28–30).

A general heading to the qualifications for overseer or elder. This expression does not mean “without sin,” which would disqualify everyone except Jesus, but “above scandalous reproach.” Paul’s overriding concern is that overseers (elders) have a good standing among both Christians and non-Christians (v. 7). On the qualifications for overseers (elders), see also Titus 1:6–9.

**the husband of one wife.** This difficult expression (v. 12; Titus 1:6; cf. 5:9) has been variously understood to prohibit polygamy, remarriage after a divorce, or marital infidelity. Given the widespread immorality in the Greco-Roman world and a similar use of the phrase at 1 Tim. 5:9, the last seems to fit Paul’s focus best. Paul is not banning single men from the office of elder, since both he and Barnabas were apparently unmarried during their ministry (1 Cor. 9:5); rather, his emphasis is that the elder’s sexual conduct must be exemplary in purity whether he is married or not.

**able to teach.** To mention the teaching competency of the overseer (elder) is important given the problem at Ephesus (5:17). Titus 1:9 indicates that elders’ firm grasp of God’s Word will enable them both to teach it and to refute errors that contradict it. Since this ability is not repeated in the qualifications for deacons, it seems that teaching the Word is one function that sets the overseer’s task apart from the deacon’s. For the general distinction between ministry of the Word and ministry of deeds in service, see Acts 6:2–4; 1 Pet. 4:10, 11.

Again, men who do not have children are not excluded from the eldership (v. 2 note); but for those who do, the attitudes of their children reflect the fruit of their spiritual management of his home and thus forecast the effect of his leadership in the church.
A general statement of the overseer’s (elder’s) responsibility.

verse_quote: not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit.
note:
For a Christian to move too quickly into this position could be an occasion for pride.

**fall into the condemnation of the devil.** Paul does not view lightly the fall of those holding this office, perhaps because some overseers in Ephesus had become involved in the false teaching (v. 1).

Deacons are officers in the church alongside overseers/elders (cf. Phil. 1:1). The precise tasks of the deacon are not spelled out in this passage. The church has usually viewed the ministry in terms of the role of the seven chosen to help the apostles in Acts 6:1–6 (specifically by tending to widows’ material needs). Although the noun “deacon” is not used in regard to the seven in that passage, a related term in that passage describes both the apostles’ “ministry of the word” and the “ministry of tables” conducted by the seven.

A term used elsewhere by Paul to refer to the revealed truth of the gospel (v. 16; Rom. 16:25, 26; 1 Cor. 2:7; 4:1; Eph. 1:9; 3:3–9; 6:19; Col. 1:26, 27; 2:2; 4:3). Perhaps some of the deacons at Ephesus had been taken in by the false teaching.

This is probably not a reference to a specific testing period, but rather a careful examination of their conduct and their commitment to sound teaching.

**prove themselves blameless.** Paul uses the same Gk. word in regard to overseers in Titus 1:6, 7; his requirement that overseers be “above reproach” in v. 2 (note) uses a Gk. synonym.

Lit. “women.” This verse abruptly interrupts the section on deacons. Its meaning is contested. The “women” are probably either the wives of the deacons or female assistants to the deacons; however, they may also be female deacons on par with the male deacons. The absence of a similar set of qualifications for the wives of elders (vv. 1–7) suggests that the women in view here, whether deacons’ wives or others, actively participate in the ministry of mercy led by the deacons (whereas elders’ wives would not share their husbands’ oversight authority). The abruptness of the insertion may reflect Paul’s concern that women, in particular, have not fared well at the hands of the false teachers (2:14; 5:15).
See note on v. 2.

Although deacons’ supportive ministries may often be unnoticed and unrecognized in the church, the apostle injects a special promise to encourage them in their faithful service. See Mark 10:43–45, where “servant” and “serve” represent Gk. terms for “deacon.”

Having provided Timothy with specific instructions on prayer, worship, and church offices, Paul now states his reason for writing the letter (see Introduction: Date and Occasion). He discusses the nature of the church and offers a poetic meditation on the work of Christ.

. Both terms connote the church’s foundational role in publicly presenting or displaying the truth before the world. Paul’s intent is to emphasize, over against the false teachers, that the truth of the gospel is found in and held out to the world by God’s church (2 Tim. 2:19). He is not imputing infallibility to the church or stating that the authority of later church leaders is equivalent to the authority of the apostles or their testimony, which now makes up the New Testament.

See note on v. 9. What follows may be a fragment of an early Christian hymn or creedal confession, composed of three balanced couplets. It certainly reflects Paul’s understanding of the person and work of Christ as the center or core of the Christian gospel (cf. 1 Cor. 15:1ff.).

**He was manifested in the flesh.** A reference to the incarnation, with a hint at Christ’s preexistence.

**vindicated by the Spirit.** A reference to Christ’s resurrection (Rom. 1:4). The point is that Christ’s resurrection “vindicated” Him (the Gk. word is the one Paul uses for “justified”) by overturning the guilty verdict of the ungodly world’s court. The world’s court judged Him to be in the wrong and a liar and false teacher, but the resurrection proved that He lived a life of perfect righteousness. Elsewhere, believers are identified with Christ’s resurrection (see Rom. 4:25) and are thus identified with His perfect righteousness as well.

**seen by angels.** A reference to the ascension (Acts 1:10, 11) and the audience that witnessed Christ’s victory in the heavenly sphere.

**proclaimed among the nations.** In the power of the Spirit who descended at Pentecost, the apostles proclaimed Christ’s glory to an international audience in the earthly sphere (Matt. 28:18–20).

**believed on in the world.** The effect of gospel proclamation in the earthly sphere is the Gentiles’ coming to faith and salvation in Christ.

**taken up in glory.** A reference to Christ’s exaltation to the right hand of God (Acts 7:56) and His present reign as Lord over all (heavenly sphere).

Returning to the purpose for which he left Timothy in Ephesus (1:3–20), Paul continues his attack on the false teachers and their teachings.

**4:1 the Spirit expressly says.** Presumably a specific revelation the Holy Spirit granted to someone, perhaps Paul himself (Acts 20:22–31; cf. 21:11).

**in later times.** This is not a future period just before the second coming of Christ. Rather, in keeping with the overall NT perspective, it is the era inaugurated by Christ’s first advent and consummated at His return (Acts 2:17; Heb. 1:2; 1 Pet. 1:20; 1 John 2:18; cf. 2 Tim. 3:1). The end-time tribulation has begun (2 Thess. 2:7; 1 John 2:18) and will get worse as the very end draws near (2 Thess. 2:3, 4).

**some will ... demons.** A reference to the false teachers, who have arisen within the church. The particular aspect of the latter-day tribulation in mind here is that of false teaching and deception.

verse_quote: forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods.
note:
The false teachers promoted a rigorous lifestyle (cf. Col. 2:20–23). Some argued that since the material world was evil, the spiritual individual should avoid it. Others inferred from the same negative view of material reality that indulging one’s sensual desires has no effect on one’s spiritual standing and identity (1 Cor. 6:14 note). It is just as demonic to repudiate the thankful and holy enjoyment of God’s material gifts as it is to abuse those gifts in ways contrary to His Word.

**foods that God created.** The following argument focuses on foods. Paul has already affirmed marriage in 3:2, 12.

verse_quote: everything created by God is good.
note: Contrary to the false teachers, the Christian affirms the essential goodness of God’s creation (Gen. 1) and therefore uses created things in the way that God commands us to use them.

Having exposed the false teachers for what they are, Paul continues with a series of personal admonitions to Timothy regarding his ministry.

**4:6 trained.** The “good servant” must be continually nourished by true doctrine in order to nourish others in that same truth.

See note on 1:4.

**train yourself for godliness.** Throughout this section, Paul intertwines spiritual discipline with official duties, invoking athletic metaphors that he uses elsewhere (2 Tim. 2:5; 4:7; 1 Cor. 9:24–27; Gal. 2:2; 5:7; Phil. 2:16).
See note on 1:15.

The general call to repentance and salvation is extended to all people (Matt. 11:28), for we do not know whom God has chosen to save but we do know that He has elected people from every tribe and tongue (Rev. 7:9–17). See theological note “Definite Atonement” on p. 1875.

**especially of those who believe.** Salvation is God’s gift, in particular to those who trust in His provision in Christ (Matt. 22:14; Rom. 8:30). The Gk. word translated “especially” may also be translated “that is to say,” as can be elsewhere in Paul’s letters. In this case, Paul clarifies that, by “all people,” he means those who come to believe in Christ. But sometimes the Gk. word may mean “especially” or “particularly,” thus referring to a smaller group that is a part of the general group previously mentioned. In this case, Paul may be using “Savior” in a broader sense as “benefactor,” as it was applied to Roman emperors: in His common grace, God lavishes generous provision on “all people” or “on the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:45); but He focuses special, redemptive grace on “those who believe.”

verse_quote: Let no one despise you for your youth.
note:
The negative commands here and in v. 14 may indicate that Timothy had a tendency towards shyness or timidity (2 Tim. 1:6–8). Furthermore, some in the church at Ephesus may not have accepted his authority (Introduction: Date and Occasion). Timothy was probably in his thirties, and therefore younger than many of the Christians (and elders) at Ephesus.

**example ... in purity.** Timothy is to establish his authority not by flaunting it or insisting upon it but by setting an example of godly living (Titus 2:7).

See 3:14, 15 and Introduction: Date and Occasion.

**devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture ... to teaching.** These are positive methods for exposing the false teaching and neutralizing its impact (cf. 1:3, 4). Not only the exposition and application of God’s Word in exhortation and teaching, but also the public reading of Scripture is a means of grace.
See note on 1:18; 2 Tim. 1:6.

A reference to the advancement of Timothy’s spiritual life, his ministry, or perhaps both. Noteworthy is the fact that it is “progress,” not arrival. Although Christians must not perform good works for the sake of gathering others’ attention and admiration (Matt. 6:1), Christ’s reputation and believers’ spiritual growth are enhanced when growing maturity can be seen in the church’s leaders and members (3:7; Col. 4:5; 1 Thess. 4:12; Titus 2:5, 7, 8, 10).

verse_quote: on yourself and on the teaching.
note:
That Paul summarizes his instructions to Timothy in this manner is an indication of where the false teachers have gone astray, and, hence, where both ministers and Christians in general can go astray, both in character and in convictions.

**you will save.** God alone grants salvation (v. 10; 1:1; 2:3), but He is pleased to use His people as instruments in bringing salvation to others. Salvation is not completed in our experience when we come to saving faith. To be sure, faith brings justification and the assurance of salvation, and having been justified, there is no doubt that we will be glorified and freed from the presence of sin, which is the consummation of our salvation (Rom. 8:28–30). Faith also begins the lifelong process of sanctification by which we are conformed to Christ that continues until the Christian’s final glorification in heaven. In other words, everyone who has been justified will certainly be sanctified and glorified, but whereas our justification is complete the moment we believe, our sanctification is an ongoing process that is not completed until we die. Even then, we do not receive our full and final glorification until the resurrection of our bodies, although in heaven we will be free of sin as we await the final resurrection (Rom. 8:1–30).

** ** not a result of works, so that no one may boast,” he is using the term “saved” as a synonym for “justified.” By grace we have been justified by faith, which is not our own doing but the gift of God and not the result of our works.

**yourself.** Sanctification is a work of God that includes the cooperative activity of the Christian. However, God’s work in His people guarantees that they will cooperate (Phil. 2:12, 13). The Lord never fails to sanctify those whom He justifies. Having changed our hearts in regeneration, our natural and inevitable response is to walk by the Spirit and put sin to death.

verse_quote: Do not rebuke an older man.
note:
A command that balances the exhortation Paul gave Timothy in 4:12. Timothy is not to abuse the authority he possesses, nor to overstep the boundaries of respect that are appropriate for those of advanced age, even when they need correction.

**encourage.** The good minister appeals to other believers with the respect owed to members of one’s family.

The final phrase almost certainly focuses on the pastor’s relationship to young women, in which increased temptations to impurity may arise. Elsewhere, Paul advises Titus to instruct older men, older women, and younger men directly; but he indicates that older women are to train the young women in godly living (Titus 2:1–8).

Paul now turns his attention to three groups in which problems had apparently arisen in the church at Ephesus: widows, elders, and slaves.

**5:3–16** Paul’s concern to identify needy widows and to provide for their proper care forms the backdrop for a discussion of the problems of younger widows, some of whom have apparently been influenced by the false teaching at Ephesus (see Introduction: Date and Occasion).

**5:3 Honor.** That is, care for as well as respect. See Mark 7:9–13.

**who are truly widows.** The care of widows, who frequently had great material needs, is a major theme in the OT (Deut. 24:19–21; Is. 1:17; Jer. 22:3; Zech. 7:9, 10; Mal. 3:5) and was a special concern of the early church (v. 16; Acts 6:1; James 1:27). Paul’s designation (“truly widows”) means that not every window is eligible for the church’s material benevolences. Women whose husbands had died but who had children or other family members to provide for them were not “truly widows” by Paul’s criteria here (vv. 4, 8, 16), but only those “left all alone” (v. 5). Also younger widows (under sixty years) who can remarry and so fulfill their callings as wives and mothers should do so, rather than being financially supported by the church (vv. 9–15).

verse_quote: But if a widow has children or grandchildren.
note: The truly needy widow had no family from which to receive support (vv. 8, 16).

Genuine poverty often drove widows to exemplary lives of prayer and faithful dependence upon God. For such widows, the church is to be the visible hand of God in providing for needs. Note the example of Anna (Luke 2:36–38).
Spiritually dead.

verse_quote: Command ... that they may be without reproach.
note: Perhaps a reference not to the whole church, but specifically to the widows.

Some have seen here an official order of widows with duties to perform (vv. 5, 10); others have seen an agreement whereby some widows provide certain services for the church in exchange for material support. More likely the list is simply of widows who are to receive support from the church (v. 16), and whose entire pattern of living has been characterized by the good works that are evidence of living faith in Christ (v. 10). This list probably consists of the larger group of widows dealt with in vv. 3–5.

**less than sixty years of age.** A round number reflecting the expectation in that culture of the age under which remarriage would still be possible (cf. vv. 11–14).

**the wife of one husband.** See note on 3:2.

The verbs in this verse are in the past tense. Paul’s concern is not with what the widow might still do for the church but with the pattern of “faith working through love” (Gal. 5:6) that has been seen throughout her life.

**washed the feet of the saints.** A conventional expression of hospitality and self-negating service in a culture where people wore sandals and walked dusty roads (cf. John 13:4, 5). Jesus commanded His disciples to wash each other’s feet (John 13:14, 15).

Lit. “when they live sensually.”

**they desire to marry.** Such a desire in younger widows is not wrong in itself, nor would remarriage necessarily “draw them away from Christ.” In fact, Paul recommends this course (v. 14). It is possible that enrollment on the list of widows is what makes subsequent remarriage a grievous offense that incurs condemnation (v. 12), so such enrollment seems to have entailed a vow of lifelong celibacy in singleness.

This may refer to a vow or pledge of celibacy that was entailed in being enrolled as a widow who would receive ongoing support from the church. Others believe that Paul is referring to younger widows’ marriage to non-Christian husbands (1 Cor. 7:39), compromising or even renouncing their basic commitment to Christ (vv. 11, 15). However, 1 Tim. 5 does not overtly address the issue of marriage to unbelievers.
Lit. “those who talk nonsense.” This is probably a reference to the false teachings (v. 15; 1:3; 4:7).
See note on 2:15.
Paul gives much attention to widows because some of the younger widows had come under the influence of the false teachers (2 Tim. 3:6, 7).

As with widows, Paul addresses the twin issues of proper honor for elders and how to deal with those who sin.

**5:17 elders.** See note on 3:1.

**double honor.** The honor befitting the position of leadership as well as financial remuneration. The Gk. term “honor,” like the English “honorarium,” can refer to a monetary amount (Acts 4:34; 19:19; 1 Cor. 6:20; 7:23). The Scriptures cited in v. 18 enjoin the financial support of the officers who teach the Word and shepherd the flock (see 1 Cor. 9:9–14; Gal. 6:6).

**especially ... teaching.** This seems to refer to two kinds of elders: those who govern the church and those who, in addition, carry out the more specialized ministry of preaching and teaching. Some elders can and should be recognized as ruling well, even though the focus of their ministry is not public exposition of Scripture. This verse is the basis of the distinction between teaching elders and ruling elders. Teaching elders, also known as ordained pastors or ministers, have the primary responsibility of teaching and preaching in their congregations. Ruling elders, on the other hand, are able to teach but spend less time teaching and preaching than teaching elders do even as ruling elders share in the responsibility of governing the church, as well as praying for and caring for the people under their watch.

That Paul cites both Deut. 25:4 (also cited in 1 Cor. 9:9) and a saying of Jesus recorded in Luke 10:7 as “Scripture” is an indication of how Christian writings that were written by the apostles or their closest associates under their authority were early understood to be on the same level of authority as the OT (2 Pet. 3:15, 16).

Throughout Scripture, an accusation of misconduct against any member of God’s community must be substantiated by testimony from multiple witnesses (Deut. 19:15; Matt. 18:16; 2 Cor. 13:1; Heb. 10:28). This standard of reliable evidence is all the more essential when charges are brought against an elder, whose office deserves special respect and whose maturity the church has (presumably) verified (3:1–7; 5:22, 24, 25).

Elders who sin (some had apparently become involved in the false teaching, although the application is wider, including character and conduct as well as the content of instruction; 4:16).

**rebuke them in the presence of all.** The influence of an elder’s example sometimes requires public rebuke to safeguard others (see Gal. 2:11–14).

Those who will presumably serve as witnesses at the judgment (cf. Matt. 25:31; Rev. 14:10).

**without prejudging.** Elders are not to be condemned on insufficient evidence; nor are they to be exempted from discipline because of their office and authority if their sin is demonstrated.

To participate in the ordination of an elder known to be unqualified is to approve of his sins and to risk sharing the guilt for them.

**keep yourself pure.** See 4:12, 16.

The practice of abstaining from wine as a matter of principle perhaps reflects the influence of the false teachers’ concept of purity (4:3).

**use a little wine ... ailments.** Paul recognizes a medicinal value of wine. Believers are free to make use of ordinary means in caring for themselves. It is no mark of faith to reject the advice of doctors or to forego medical treatment.

Although Timothy, other elders, and church members cannot see into others’ hearts, the spiritual state of the heart eventually comes to light, for ill or for good. Therefore, the church should call its officers on the basis of their observed behavior, and those officers should hold each other accountable based on what they seen in the actions of one another.

**The sins of some people ... judgment.** Another reference to the importance of care in screening candidates for ordination., 25

Paul addresses the problem of slaves who have not been showing proper respect for their Christian masters.

**6:1 under a yoke.** Paul gives instructions to slaves in Eph. 6:5–8; Col. 3:22–25; and Titus 2:9, 10.

**the teaching.** Presumably, this is in contrast to the false teaching, which may have encouraged insubordination among some of the Christian slaves.

Paul returns one last time to the problem of the false teachers, noting especially their divisiveness and their greed. This leads him to reflect upon the proper perspective one should have on material possessions.

verse_quote: controversy and for quarrels about words.
note: Contentiousness was one of the prominent characteristics of the false teachers (1:4; 2 Tim. 2:14, 23; Titus 3:9).
Perhaps some of the false teachers were seeking the position of elder out of greed (v. 10; Titus 1:11).

Christians can be content because their needs are met by Christ (2 Cor. 12:9, 10; Phil. 4:11, 13).

**great gain.** The gain that godliness brings is not financial, since such profit is short-lived and cannot be taken along when we leave this world at death (v. 7). As Timothy is to show those who are financially wealthy, being “rich in good works” means treasuring up “a good foundation” for an eternal future (vv. 17–19).

verse_quote: we brought nothing into the world.
note: Paul may allude to Job’s expression of submission to God’s hard providence when wealth and family were stripped away from him.
The desire for wealth, like the quest for prominence (3:6, 7) and stubborn resistance to truth (2 Tim. 2:25, 26), poses a trap, disguising lethal danger behind appealing appearances.

verse_quote: some have wandered away from the faith.
note: See note on v. 5.
As he has done previously, Paul follows his comments about the false teachers with personal exhortations to Timothy, concluding with a marvelous doxology.

verse_quote: Fight the good fight of the faith.
note:
A metaphor for the Christian life viewed in terms of faithfulness to Christ (2 Tim. 4:7).

**Take hold of the eternal life.** That is, do not become complacent. While faith in Christ begins new life (4:8), the goal of the Christian life is always future (v. 19; 1:16 note; Phil. 3:12; 2 Tim. 4:8).

**to which you were called.** Eternal life is not something we naturally choose, but something to which God supernaturally calls us (Rom. 8:30).

**good confession in the presence of many witnesses.** This probably refers to Timothy’s baptism. The “good confession” that one has come to faith in Christ leads naturally into the “good fight” of seeking to live in faithfulness to Him.

verse_quote: before Pontius Pilate made the good confession.
note: This may refer to Jesus’ trial before Pilate (Matt. 27:11; Mark 15:2; Luke 23:3; John 18:33–37; 19:8–11), but it may be an allusion to His calm and voluntary death as well.

Probably a reference to all that Paul has charged concerning Timothy’s personal discipline and official duties.

**the appearing.** The second coming of Christ (2 Tim. 4:1, 8; Titus 2:13).

verse_quote: King of kings and Lord of lords.
note: This expression is applied to Christ in Rev. 19:16; cf. 17:14.

verse_quote: who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see.
note: As spirit, God is “invisible” to our physical eyes (1:17). Yet God condescends to make His glory visible to sinful human beings while at the same time shielding them from the full manifestation of His divine being, lest they be destroyed by His consuming holiness (Gen. 32:30; Ex. 24:10, 11; 33:18–23; Num. 12:6–8; Is. 6:1–5). Paul refers here to the overpowering radiance of God’s divine being in Himself, which we His sinful creatures cannot perceive apart from the mediation of Christ the divine Son (John 1:18; Rev. 22:3–5). In glory, however, once all sin has been removed from us, we will see the Lord as He is and view Him face to face (1 Cor. 13:12; 1 John 3:2).

Having condemned the love of money and affirmed the future orientation of Christian hope, Paul provides an exhortation for those who do find themselves rich in this world (presumably not from greed).

**6:17 to enjoy.** Christ does not demand that every believer embrace abject poverty and ascetic self-denial. See note on 4:4.

The financial wealth of prosperous Christians is not merely for their personal consumption, but provides resources for them to amass eternal “riches” through generous sharing with others. God blesses His people so that they may be a blessing to others.

See Matt. 6:20.

**take hold of that which is truly life.** See note on v. 12. Generous distribution of one’s wealth to meet others’ needs does not earn eternal life, but it demonstrates that one’s hope has been transferred from “the uncertainty of riches” and placed instead on God, the lavish giver (v. 17).

Paul brings the letter to a close with one final charge to Timothy, once again set within the context of dealing with the false teachers.

**6:20 the deposit entrusted to you.** That is, the sound doctrine of the gospel (1:10, 11). Timothy is a trustee of God’s invaluable treasure, charged to maintain it undamaged and to entrust it unmodified into the custody of future generations of faithful stewards (2 Tim. 1:14; 2:2).

**what is falsely called “knowledge.”** The false teachers emphasize “knowledge” (Gk. _gnōsis,_ from which the word Gnosticism is derived; see Introduction to 2 Timothy: Special Issues). Paul began his letter by addressing false teaching (1:3–7), and here in vv. 20 and 21 he concludes the epistle by once more addressing false teaching. Thus, the letter is bounded by the conceptual bookends of false teaching, which shows that false teaching is the main occasion that inspired Paul to write this letter. Accordingly, much of what is said in this letter is, in one way or another, related to aspects of the false teaching (on which, see especially the comment on 4:3–4).

**6:21 Grace be with you.** This abrupt conclusion, lacking Paul’s usual personal greetings, suggests that Paul saw the situation he was addressing to be quite serious. Some of the earliest Gk. manuscripts have the plural form of “you” (as in 2 Tim. 4:22; Titus 3:15) in this benediction, indicating that Paul intended for the letter to be read to the entire church even though its primary addressee is Timothy.
